title: Cap. II Arg. 6: James 2:5 — poor elect / rich in faith grounds foresight-election
latin: Sextum testimonium quo nititur Vasques, habetur Jacob. ii. 5. Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo, divites in fide, & heredes regni, quod promisit Deus diligentibus se? Hoc est, interprete Jesuita, Deus eos qui in hoc mundo pauperes erant, quia erant in fide & charitate divites, elegit ad gloriam, sive regni hereditatem. Electio igitur ad gloriam est ex praescientia Dei, qui videt quinam tandem futuri sunt divites in fide & operibus.
pass_a: The sixth testimony on which Vasquez rests is found in James 2:5: Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which God has promised to those who love him? This is, the Jesuit interprets, God chose those who were poor in this world, because they were rich in faith and charity, unto glory, or the inheritance of the kingdom. Election to glory is therefore from the foreknowledge of God, who sees who at last will be rich in faith and works.
pass_b: Sixth: Vasquez leans on James 2:5 — "Has not God chosen the poor in this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him?" The Jesuit reads it: God chose those who were poor in this world because they were rich in faith and charity — chose them to glory, the inheritance of the kingdom. So, they say, election to glory hangs on God's foresight of who will finally be rich in faith and works.

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: scopus — do not despise the poor; 1 Cor. 1:26 parallel
latin: Scopus verborum hic est; Pauperes non esse a nobis contemnendos, quia tantum abest ut negligantur a Deo, ut in dispensatione rerum spiritualium maximam ob partem praeferantur ditioribus: Divites e contra non esse nimis suspiciendos, & cum neglectu pauperum honorandos, quia Deus saepenumero vacuos dimittit divites, cum pauperes impleat bonis. Non absimilis huic est ille alter locus 1 Cor. i. 26. Non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles: Sed quae stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia, &c. Ostendit ergo Apostolus Deum ex classe pauperum plures elegisse, quos tum fide tum hereditate caelesti donaret, quam ex numero divitum.
pass_a: The scope of the words is this: the poor are not to be despised by us, because so far are they from being neglected by God that in the dispensation of spiritual things they are for the most part preferred to the richer; the rich, on the contrary, are not to be overly looked up to and honored with neglect of the poor, because God often sends the rich away empty while he fills the poor with goods. Not unlike this is that other place, 1 Corinthians 1:26: Not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble: but the foolish things of the world God has chosen to confound the strong, etc. The Apostle therefore shows that God has chosen more from the class of the poor, whom he would gift with both faith and heavenly inheritance, than from the number of the rich.
pass_b: Reply: James's point is that we must not despise the poor. Far from neglecting them, God in spiritual gifts mostly prefers them to the richer. The rich, for their part, are not to be overrated and honored while the poor are ignored — God often sends the rich away empty and fills the poor with goods. 1 Corinthians 1:26 runs the same way: not many wise by flesh, not many mighty, not many noble — God chose what the world calls foolish to shame the strong. So the Apostle shows God has chosen more from the poor, to give them faith and the heavenly inheritance, than from the rich.

lemmas.gloss: more elect from poor than rich

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: conjungit — elect to become rich in faith, not because foreseen rich
latin: Atque hinc est quod conjungit haec duo, divites in fide, & heredes regni. Non dixit electos heredes regni, quia praevisi erant futuri divites in fide, sed electi erant ut fierent divites in fide, atque heredes regni.
pass_a: And hence it is that he joins these two, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom. He did not say the elect are heirs of the kingdom because they were foreseen as going to be rich in faith, but they were elect that they might become rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom.
pass_b: That is why he binds the two phrases: rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom. He did not say the elect are heirs because they were foreseen as going to be rich in faith. He said they were elect so they would become rich in faith — and heirs of the kingdom.

lemmas.gloss: elect unto faith-richness, not from foresight

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: Vasquez calumny — if elect=make rich, then elect=make poor?
latin: Hanc expositionem frivola calumniatione Vasques conatur evertere: Si, inquit, eligere divitem in fide est facere divitem in fide, eligere etiam pauperes in hoc mundo, erit facere pauperes in hoc mundo: at Jacobus non significavit Deum fecisse pauperes, sed eos qui pauperes erant, quia fuerunt divites in fide, elegisse ad gloriam. Respondeo, nullum absurdum inde sequi si dicamus Deum fecisse pauperes in hoc mundo, cum ipsa distinctio pauperum & divitum fiat ex decreto voluntatis Divinae; sed fatemur non ea spectare verba Apostoli; neque hoc obstat interpretationi nostrae;
pass_a: Vasquez tries to overturn this exposition by a frivolous calumny: If, he says, to choose a rich man in faith is to make him rich in faith, then to choose the poor in this world will also be to make them poor in this world; but James did not signify that God made people poor, but that those who were poor, because they were rich in faith, he chose unto glory. I answer: no absurdity follows if we say God made the poor in this world, since the very distinction of poor and rich comes from the decree of the Divine will; but we admit that the Apostle's words do not look to that; nor does this hinder our interpretation;
pass_b: Vasquez tries a cheap jab at that reading: if "choosing the rich in faith" means making them rich in faith, then "choosing the poor in this world" would mean making them poor — yet James does not say God made people poor; he says those who already were poor, because they were rich in faith, God chose to glory. Reply: no absurdity if we say God made people poor in this world — the rich/poor split itself comes from the divine decree. We grant James's words are not about that. And that does not hurt our reading;

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: fishermen analogy — elect makes apostles/faithful, not prior trade/poverty
latin: quod exemplo non dissimili patebit. Si dicamus Deum elegisse piscatores Apostolos suos, in hac loquendi formula eligere est idem quod facere Apostolum; non autem significat facere piscatores, quia prius sua voluntate erant facti piscatores, quam electi Apostoli: Sic cum dico Deum elegisse pauperes divites in fide & heredes regni, eligere est idem quod facere fideles & regni heredes, sed non est idem quod facere pauperes; quia tum supponuntur pauperes cum donantur fide & adoptione ad regnum coeleste.
pass_a: which will be clear from a not dissimilar example. If we say God chose fishermen as his Apostles, in this way of speaking "to choose" is the same as "to make an Apostle"; it does not, however, signify "to make fishermen," because by their own will they had already been made fishermen before they were elect Apostles. So when I say God chose the poor rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, "to choose" is the same as "to make believers and heirs of the kingdom," but it is not the same as "to make them poor"; because then they are supposed already poor when they are gifted with faith and adoption unto the heavenly kingdom.
pass_b: a near parallel shows why. If we say God chose fishermen as his Apostles, "choose" there means make them Apostles — not make them fishermen. They were already fishermen by their own trade before they were elect Apostles. So when I say God chose the poor who are rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom, "choose" means make them believers and kingdom-heirs — not make them poor. Poverty is already assumed when faith and adoption to the heavenly kingdom are given.

lemmas.gloss: poverty presupposed, not produced by elect

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6: Augustine — elect makes rich in faith as he makes heirs
latin: Denique ad pleniorem verborum intelligentiam accedat & hoc quoque; Quamvis Deus non eligat homines ex praescientia fidei, recte tamen dicitur elegisse divites in fide, quia tales facit in tempore eos omnes, quos elegit ab aeterno; & quia tales factos jam actualiter & quasi visibiliter eligit, & ab infidelibus secretos in peculium suum transfert. Concludamus hoc responsum verbis illis quibus Augustinus hunc ipsum locum explicavit; Elegit Deus fideles, sed ut fiant, non quia jam erant. Eligendo ergo facit divites in fide, sicut heredes regni. Recte quippe in eis hoc eligere dicitur, quod ut in eis faciat, eos elegit. Haec ille, De Praedest. Sanct. lib. 1. cap. 17.
pass_a: Finally, for a fuller understanding of the words let this also be added: although God does not elect men from foresight of faith, he is rightly said to have chosen those rich in faith, because in time he makes such all those whom he elected from eternity; and because, having made them such, he already actually and as it were visibly elects them, and transfers them, set apart from unbelievers, into his own peculiar people. Let us close this reply with those words by which Augustine explained this very place: God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By electing, therefore, he makes them rich in faith, just as he makes them heirs of the kingdom. Rightly indeed is this choosing said in them, that what he may do in them, he chose them. So he, On the Predestination of the Saints, book 1, chapter 17.
pass_b: Add this for the full sense: God does not elect from foresight of faith, yet he is rightly said to have chosen the rich in faith — because in time he makes such everyone he elected from eternity; and because, once made such, he already actually and almost visibly elects them, sets them apart from unbelievers, and takes them as his own. Close with Augustine on this very text (On the Predestination of the Saints 1.17): "God chose the faithful, but that they might become so, not because they already were. By electing he makes them rich in faith, just as he makes them heirs of the kingdom." That choosing is rightly said of them: he chose them so that he might do this in them.

lemmas.lemma: Elegit ... ut fiant, non quia jam erant

lemmas.gloss: electing makes rich in faith = heirs

title: Cap. II Sol. Arg. 6 close: not elect because foreseen faithful — foresight because electing makes them
latin: Non ergo Deus elegit quia praevidit illos futuros fideles, sed praevisi sunt fideles quia eligendo eos tales facit.
pass_a: God therefore did not elect because he foresaw that they would be faithful, but they were foreseen as faithful because by electing them he makes them such.
pass_b: Bottom line: foresight of future faith is not why God elects. He foresaw them faithful because election itself is what makes them faithful.

lemmas.gloss: foresight not the cause of elect
